16695-fighting-instructions-1530-1816-pu:
Julian S. Corbett edited this volume twenty-nine of the Navy Records Society, printed in 1905, gathering fighting instructions from 1530 to 1816. He adds notes from writers of the time to explain each set of orders. The council list names the Prince of Wales as patron, Earl Spencer as president, and many admirals and scholars.

Corbett shows how sea battle orders grew from loose sailing rules into tight fleet tactics over nearly three centuries. Each document gives the words captains actually sailed by, with context for why they changed. Naval buffs and history readers will find a prime source book, best used beside a plain history of sea war for its full sense.
20627-torchy-private-sec:
Torchy, Private Sec. finds Sewell Ford's office boy promoted. Torchy now serves as private secretary, but he tells the story in the same slang as ever. He begins by recalling his old place behind the brass rail, at the jump end of the buzzer.

I was everybody's slave in general, he says, and Piddie's football in particular. You know: head office boy of the Corrugated Trust. From that low stool he has risen to the private secretary's desk. The comedy follows Torchy through deals, bosses, and his courtship of Vee, with New York office life as the stage.
23779-a-little-girl-in-old-quebec:
Amanda M. Douglas published A Little Girl in Old Quebec in 1906, a companion to her old New York and old Boston books. Its heroine is Rose, a wild rose of a girl. Its hero is Ralph Destournier, who climbs Quebec's crags whistling a French song and wondering what led Samuel de Champlain to dream a city on so rocky a spot.

Below the cliffs, a few rough wooden buildings mark the lower town, walled and loopholed for musketry. Chapters follow Rose through friendship, summer time, marriages, and a lover in earnest, to the passing of old Quebec. Douglas blends a girl's story with the heroic beginnings of a famous fortress city.
25184-a-dissertation-on-the-medical-prop:
A. McAllister's Dissertation on the Medical Properties and Injurious Effects of Tobacco, read before the Oneida County Medical Society in January 1830, warns against habitual tobacco use. The second edition of 1832 adds an introductory preface by Moses Stuart of Andover.

McAllister argues from digestion and the body's economy, asking what becomes of a man who keeps his quid in his mouth through meals and swallows saliva steeped in poison. He allows that some heavy users eat well, but notes that many grow thin. The essay is an early American medical attack on a common habit.
26097-submission-to-divine-providence-in:
P. Doddridge's sermon, preached at Northampton on the death of a child about five years old, urges mourning parents toward submission to divine providence. Published out of compassion to such parents, the second edition of 1740 opens with a preface on the preacher's own grief for a child whose temper matched his own.

Doddridge argues that a child's death warns the living of their own mortality, since all flesh is as grass and its glory like the flower of the field. When the house becomes a house of mourning, he writes, parents should lay the loss to heart and be quickened by it. The sermon closes with a postscript, offering doctrine and comfort in one short discourse.
28740-the-girls-of-central-high-in-camp-:
Gertrude W. Morrison's The Girls of Central High in Camp, or The Old Professor's Secret, published by the Saalfield Publishing Company with copyright 1915, plans a summer. Bobby Hargrew, Laura Belding, Jess Morse, the Lockwood twins, and Nellie Agnew, juniors with an athletic record, debate where to spend vacation. No seashore resort, they agree, with its slogan of sun, sand, and skeeter-bites, and its cost.

Jess, whose play awaits professional production next season, needs her mother as chaperon, and her mother wants a quiet spot to write a book. Chapters follow visitors' day, Lonesome Liz, the start, the camp on Acorn Island, a kleptomaniantic ghost, and a sheriff with dogs. Professor Dimp and the barnacle's nose lead to the old professor's secret.
29754-whittier-land-a-handbook-of-north-:
Samuel T. Pickard, author of Life and Letters of John Greenleaf Whittier, wrote Whittier-Land, a handbook of North Essex, printed by Houghton Mifflin of Boston and New York. It gathers many anecdotes of and poems by Whittier never before collected, with pictures from photographs: Haverhill, Haverhill Academy, Main Street, and the poet's birthplace in winter. An ambrotype of Whittier from about 1857 fronts the book.

Pickard walks the reader through the country that made the poet, town by town, house by house. The handbook serves pilgrims to Whittier's land as well as readers of his verse. Lovers of Whittier will find a fond, well-illustrated guide to the poet's home ground.
29971-old-groans-and-new-songs-being-med:
F. C. Jennings wrote Old Groans and New Songs, meditations on the Book of Ecclesiastes, printed in New York, Glasgow, and London in 1920. Jennings warns in his preface that readers should expect no more than is intended. The notes are meditations of a devotional rather than a critical character, jotted down during private morning readings of the Scriptures.

Month by month the subject opened so far that, by the end, Jennings felt a distinct need to rewrite the earlier chapters entirely. He sends the book forth in its original shape instead, so the reader may share his delight at ever-new beauties in the landscape at each turn of the road. One point gets closer treatment in the preface: the authorship of Ecclesiastes, and the strong attack made on Solomon's authorship by what Jennings calls the ecclesiastical infidelity of the day.
3876-memoirs-of-the-courts-of-louis-xv-a:
Madame du Hausset, lady's maid to Madame de Pompadour, wrote the memoirs that open this collection on the courts of Louis the Fifteenth and Sixteenth. An advertisement from the London Magazine calls them the only perfectly sincere memoirs of the reign. Du Hausset mistakes through ignorance but never misleads, unlike Campan, who keeps secrets, or Lauzun and Talleyrand, who invent from vanity. The claim sets the tone for a plain spoken witness.

Court scenes show the machinery of favor. The Chevalier d'Henin walks beside a sedan chair with his lady's cloak on his arm, ready to cover her shoulders and wait in the antechamber. A cousin soon begs du Hausset to win her husband a company of horse. Readers who like backstairs views of Pompadour's court will find a candid and unadorned guide.
3877-memoirs-of-the-courts-of-louis-xv-a:
Madame du Hausset's second book opens on an evening when Pompadour, her intimate ladies at Paris and Gontaut ill, sends for her maid to read aloud. The king stays late at council over parliament's affairs, and Pompadour, vexed by a brother's letter, talks openly as she does only in anger. Her brother refuses a marriage she arranged and pledged her word to, calling the bride's parents insupportably haughty and the girl badly educated and contemptuous of the match.

Later pages weigh Pompadour's peak of influence, when Choiseul joined the ministry with her constant support since the days of Bernis. She made the Treaty of Sienna, praised the empress and Kaunitz, and talked foreign affairs with the king. Readers who like Pompadour through her maid's eyes will find politics and family pride in one voice.
3878-memoirs-of-the-courts-of-louis-xv-a:
The third book of these secret court memoirs comes from an unknown English girl who served the Princesse de Lamballe and kept her papers. The writer, placed by the Duke of Norfolk and Lady Mary Duncan, became depositary of conversations and documents of great importance, and reluctantly tells her own story to prove them genuine. Her patroness Lamballe stands at the center, with the queen's household around her.

Later passages show Marie Antoinette visiting in simple dress, without ceremony or guards, and courtiers complaining that such ease hurts French manufactures and trade. The queen answers that her state dresses shall be as brilliant as any former queen's, but appeals to her grandpapa for freedom in private. Readers who like the Revolution from inside will find a loyal and anxious witness.
3879-memoirs-of-the-courts-of-louis-xv-a:
The fourth book of these secret memoirs opens with the accession of Louis the Sixteenth and Marie Antoinette on May 10, 1774, under the most propitious auspices. After the long corrupt reign of an old debauched prince, France expects cheering change from a successor known for virtue and a consort famed for charm. The whole court moves from Versailles to La Muette in the Bois de Boulogne, near Paris, as a new reign begins.

A domestic tale shows the period's morals. A wife, advised that the best way to keep a husband home is a handmaid under the same roof, retains the Comtesse Diane in her family. Diane stays until October 17, 1789, when she leaves Versailles with the Polignacs and Artois for Italy. Readers who like the reign's hopeful dawn and its gathering dusk will find both in this volume.
3880-memoirs-of-the-courts-of-louis-xv-a:
The fifth book of these secret memoirs follows the Princesse de Lamballe's notes on Marie Antoinette's motherhood and the Diamond Necklace Affair. Lamballe, less assiduous at court as the queen's intimacy with Polignac grew, still attends the accouchement. She agrees to stand near the doctor Vermond, ready to cry in Italian that a son is born if a dauphin arrives. The queen is foiled even in this hope, being delivered of the Duchesse d'Angouleme in December 1778.

The necklace chapters show a prince confronted with the queen face to face, undone when he sees her fuller person and longer face beside the guilty D'Oliva who played her at Trianon. All he can stammer is that he will pay the jewelers Bassange. Readers who like the Revolution's prologue will find gossip turning to scandal here.
3881-memoirs-of-the-courts-of-louis-xv-a:
The sixth book of these secret memoirs carries the Lamballe papers into the Revolution's street fighting. Necker's dismissal irritates the people beyond description, mob follows mob, and the Duke of Orleans works at secret destruction. When a sabre severs his bust's head in a rising, superstitious rioters shrink back, and Penthievre warns him the omen foretells his own head and his family's ruin.

The Bastille falls on July 14, arms come from the Invalides pensioners, and fifty thousand livres pass to the chiefs who sway them. The English girl narrator, applauded through the Tuileries gardens as La Brave Anglaise, finds the queen at needlework. Readers who like the Revolution from a lady's papers will find terror and comedy mixed.
3882-memoirs-of-the-courts-of-louis-xv-a:
The seventh book of these secret memoirs, continued by an editor from the papers of the Princesse de Lamballe, faces the emigration and the Revolution's hardening. Lamballe, returning from England, had hoped the recall of emigrants would help, but the flight of the powerful struck a deathblow to the monarchy. Servants left to keep their masters' places made laws to exclude those who had resigned the sway uncalled for.

The editor argues that constitutionalists and royalists, working as two separate interests, left the monarchy at the mercy of Jacobins who hated both as former oppressors. Plans framed by the revolutionaries, he warns, are too well grounded to be defeated by divided foes. Readers who like the Revolution argued from the losing side will find a passionate and partisan book.
3883-memoirs-of-the-courts-of-louis-xv-a:
This complete text gathers the whole arc of the du Hausset and Lamballe memoirs, from Pompadour's antechamber to the Temple prison. The advertisement's claim for du Hausset's perfect sincerity opens the set, and the papers then follow favor, marriage, and revolution through two reigns. A bride's voice breaks through near the middle, mourning comfort plucked by the roots when her sister-in-law married the future Philippe Egalite.

Religion and philosophy remain her only remedies, she writes, after becoming a bride in infancy, a wife before womanhood, and a widow before motherhood. The complete memoirs suit readers who want the full journey in one file, with Pompadour's maid yielding to Lamballe's friend as the monarchy falls.
4904-quotations-from-the-project-gutenbe:
This volume gathers quotations drawn from Project Gutenberg editions, assembled by editor David Widger as a finding aid for readers. Each extract points back to its source file, so a striking passage can be traced to its full context with a short search in the original book.

The contents range widely, with multiple volumes of Meredith's Shaving of Shagpat among the early entries. The book works best as a sampler and a reference tool: browse for memorable lines, then follow them home to the works they came from. It is a collection of fragments by design, not a single narrative.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-bec:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Bec describes the Benedictine Abbey of Bec, or Le Bec, in Normandy. Herluin, a Norman knight, founded it early in the eleventh century. Herluin quit Count Gilbert of Brionne's court about 1031 for a religious life, and the modern name Bec-Hellouin preserves his memory.

Herluin's first house at Bonneville, built in 1034, moved about 1040 to a site by the Bec brook that gave the abbey its name. About two years later Lanfranc, already famous for lectures at Avranches, came to lose himself in this lowly house of prayer. The entry follows Bec's rise to fame as a school of learning under Herluin and Lanfranc, and notes that the abbey itself now lies in ruins.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jerome-hermes:
Jérôme-Hermès Bolsec, a theologian and physician probably born at Paris and dead at Lyons about 1584, began as a Carmelite monk whose Paris sermon raised doubts about his soundness. Leaving the Church about 1545, he married at Ferrara's court and turned to medicine, settling near Geneva about 1550.

Bolsec called Calvin's predestination absurd and in 1551 interrupted a Geneva Friday discussion to argue against it. Calvin's sway made the clash decisive: Bolsec was arrested and banished from Geneva forever, then driven from Thonon in 1555. Refused a Reformed ministry at Paris for want of orthodoxy, and unwilling to sign Bern's confession at Lausanne, he drifted back to France.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-laval-univers:
Laval University of Quebec was founded in 1852 by Quebec's seminary, under a royal charter from Queen Victoria signed at Westminster on 8 December 1852. Pius IX's bull Inter varias sollicitudines of 15 April 1876 gave it canonical erection and wide privileges, with the Propaganda prefect as protector at Rome.

Doctrine and discipline rest with a superior council of Quebec province's archbishop and bishops, chaired by Quebec's archbishop, who serves as chancellor. The charter makes the archbishop visitor with veto over regulations and appointments, and gives the rectorship by right to Quebec seminary's superior, elected for three years and capped at six consecutive years. Four faculties, theology, law, medicine, and arts, each with its own council, complete the structure.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-montagnais-in:
Montagnais, French for Mountaineers, is the shared name for bands speaking dialects of one Algonquian tongue. They range along the Saint Lawrence River and Gulf, from near the Saint Maurice to Cape Whittle and inland to the watershed. They are close kin to the Naskapi, who roam farther into Labrador yet use the same missions and trading posts.

Champlain met bands at the Saguenay mouth in 1603. They included the Attikamegue or Whitefish, the Kakouchac or Porcupine of Lake Saint John, and the Tadousac and Bersiamite peoples. Without farming or pottery, they lived by hunting and fishing in birchbark lodges and canoes. Polygamy prevailed, with divorce at will and descent through the mother. Recollet missionary Jean d'Albeau began regular work among them in 1615, and later Jesuits carried it on.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-cholon:
Pierre Cholonec was a French Jesuit missionary and biographer among Canada's Indians, born in Finistère on 29 June 1641. He entered the Society at Paris in 1659, taught at Moulins and Eu, studied philosophy at La Flèche and theology at Paris, and sailed for Canada in August 1674. For many years he served at St. Francis Xavier du Sault.

There the saintly Indian maiden Catherine Tegakwitha died, and Cholonec wrote her life, published in the Lettres édifiantes in 1781 and 1839, with an abridged translation in Kip's Jesuit Missions of 1846. The fuller biography survives in the Jesuit archives at Montreal. In later years Cholonec became superior of the Jesuit residence at Montreal. He died at Quebec on 30 October 1723.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-province-of-q:
Quebec province fills this encyclopedia entry with geography first. It holds the broad basin of the Saint Lawrence River, lying between the Laurentian and Alleghany ranges. It runs from the 45th to the 54th parallel, and from the 57th to the 79th meridian. Its area, 354,873 square miles, nearly equals the United Kingdom, France, Belgium and Holland combined. No land of its size holds so many generous waterways.

From land the entry turns to schooling. A council shared out limited public funds for primary and classical schools. It proposed teachers for training colleges, and it approved or rejected every textbook. Its powers were more advisory than lawmaking, since nearly all its decisions needed government sanction. A parallel committee watched over the Protestant minority's schools. The piece thus pairs a physical portrait of Quebec with the machinery of its divided, church-linked education system.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-quebec:
The Archdiocese of Quebec, in Canada, covers a string of counties, and this long encyclopedia entry follows it from mission days to the twentieth century. The Récollets came in 1615 to 1629 and the Jesuits in 1625, answering directly to the Holy See. The Jesuits returned alone in 1632, and the Archbishop of Rouen stretched his jurisdiction over the country. By the Bull of erection in 1674, the See of Quebec embraced all French possessions in North America.

That vast charge ran from Newfoundland to Louisiana, a territory larger than Europe. After the Treaty of Paris in 1783, the bishop kept Newfoundland and what became the Dominion of Canada. Later bishops consecrated new prelates, McDonell in 1820, McEachern and Lartigue in 1821, and Provencher in 1822. One archbishop ordained 114 priests, preserved Nicolet college, backed Saint Hyacinth College, fought Protestant control of schooling, and helped block the union of the Canadas in 1822.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-renee-theophi:
René-Théophile-Hyacinthe Laennec, French physician, was born at Quimper in Brittany on 17 February 1781 and died at Kerlouanec on 13 August 1826. He discovered auscultation and fathered modern knowledge of lung diseases. His father was a lawyer of literary bent whose poems recalled his compatriot De Forges Maillard. After his mother died when he was six, the boy lived with his grand-uncle, the Abbé Laennec.

At twelve he went to Nantes, where his uncle, Doctor Laennec, taught in the university faculty of medicine. He studied brilliantly, won prizes, learned English and German thoroughly, and began medicine under his uncle. At nineteen he went to Paris in 1800 and within a year took first prizes in both medicine and surgery there. His great work, De l'auscultation médiate, appeared in Paris in 1819.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tehuantepec:
Tehuantepec is a Mexican diocese, suffragan of Oaxaca, covering the southern parts of Oaxaca and Vera Cruz across the isthmus. Its people number about 202,000, and the bishop's city holds 10,000. Burgoa records from old Zapotec pictures how the king, pressed to sacrifice to Guiscipocoche, announced that white men from the sunrise would soon drive the great god out. They would conquer all kings, bring misery, and bring priests to whom survivors must confess on bended knees.

On 24 April 1522, Fray Bartolomé de Olmedo arrived with Pedro de Alvarado. King Cosijopii, a kinsman of Montezuma, welcomed them, embraced the faith, and later built the convent of S. Domingo at his own expense. Franciscans and Dominicans, including Las Casas, preached the Gospel there. A later plot by Cosijopii's descendants to return to paganism was quickly suppressed. The territory belonged to Oaxaca from 1535 until Leo XIII made it a separate see in 1891.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-ursulines:
North America's oldest school for women, Quebec's Ursuline monastery, opens its history here on 1 August 1639. That day its first members landed in Canada, thirty-one years after Champlain founded Quebec in 1608 and only four after his death. Marie de l'Incarnation, declared Venerable in 1874, and Madame de la Peltrie, a rich Norman widow, established the house.

Marie, widowed ten years before joining the Ursulines at Tours, won Bossuet's praise as the Theresa of her time and of the New World. Her son Dom Claude Martin, a Benedictine, wrote her life, approved in 1677 by Bishop Laval. Royal letters signed by Louis XIII in 1639 sanctioned the foundation, and after three years in the Lower Town the nuns entered their lasting convent in 1642.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-three-rivers-:
The Diocese of Three Rivers, in Quebec, was formed from the Archdiocese of Quebec on 8 June 1852. At first it covered Champlain and St. Maurice counties on the north shore of the St. Lawrence, with Yamaska, Nicolet, Drummond and part of Sherbrooke on the south. Later divisions carved out Sherbrooke and Pontiac, and in July 1885 the southern parishes became the Diocese of Nicolet.

The diocese then held forty-three parishes and eight missions, with 84,000 Catholics and only 800 others. Its first bishop, Thomas Cooke, died in 1870 and was followed by Louis-Francois Lafleche, who ruled until 1898. The third bishop, F.-X. Cloutier, born in 1848 and consecrated in July 1899, led a diocese served by a hundred secular priests, with Franciscan and Oblate houses and many schools.

govdocs-archive_org-the-day-after-roswel: An anthology gathers material around Philip Corso's The Day After Roswell, opening with a preface. Corso's 1997 book claimed the Army farmed alien technology out to industry. The anthology expands that UFO classic with further pieces on the same theme. For readers of Roswell literature, it collects the argument and its surrounding matter in one volume, so the case can be read whole rather than in fragments.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_nuclear-:
President Eisenhower's Atoms for Peace program promised to spread nuclear technology for civilian good. In 1955 an Atomic Energy Commission official judged it, in private, a threat to peace. This briefing book, posted in July 2019, presents documentation from a new digital Archive volume on global proliferation.

The volume carries new detail on the clandestine nuclear programs of India, China, Israel, and other would-be nuclear states. The tension is built into the subject: sharing reactors and training spread skills that weapons programs later used. An insider calling the flagship program a threat, at the time, gives that tension an official voice.
memoirs-of-the-courts-of-louis-xv-and-xv:
Madame Du Hausset's secret memoirs appear here in a complete set. She was lady's maid to Madame de Pompadour at court. The set adds the tale of an English girl and the Princess Lamballe.

An old review at the front calls her tales the most sincere of all. She may err through lack of knowledge, the review says. But she never wilfully misleads, nor hides a secret for pride. That praise sets her apart from Campan, Roland, and Lauzun in print. Pictures of the Princess Lamballe and the Queen's last ride close the list. Servant and princess speak from inside the palace walls.

Volume one of the secret memoirs of Louis XV and XVI opens the set. Madame Du Hausset, lady's maid to Pompadour, stands as its source. A list of pictures names Louis the Fifteenth and Marie Antoinette.

An old London Magazine review heads the volume as its warrant. It calls Du Hausset's memoirs the only perfectly sincere ones known. She may mistake facts through ignorance, it grants from the start. But vanity never leads her to invent, as it led Lauzun and others. That warrant of trust is the volume's chief claim to readers. A maid's plain view of Pompadour's court is its rare gift.

Book two of Du Hausset's secret memoirs opens in Pompadour's rooms. Madame sends for her maid at seven to read aloud. A letter from her brother breaks the calm of that night.

He begs her to break a match she had pledged for him. The bride's kin, he says, spoke of them both with contempt. Pompadour will not yield, and treats him coldly that Sunday. Two months later, the bride's conduct proves the brother right in full. Talk turns to why Pompadour hates the Jesuits so fiercely. Her maid holds her tongue, though court talk runs hot around her.

Book three of the secret memoirs turns to Louis XVI's court. A new narrator tells how she came by her papers. She served the Princesse de Lamballe in a confidential post for years.

Her facts came from the princess's talk and private papers alike. Born in England, she was schooled at a Paris convent in Rue du Bac. Sacchini, the Queen's own music master, taught her there as a child. Her skill drew the Queen and the princess to hear her play. Her German master and Sacchini both called her tongue native true. Music opens doors that birth alone had kept shut for her.

Book four of the secret memoirs opens at section five, in 1774. Louis XVI and Marie Antoinette take the crown on May 10. Their rise came under the most hopeful signs, the text says.

After a long, corrupt reign, France looked for pure change. The young King's known virtues won trust across the land. Crowds hailed the pair at La Muette for days on end. Joy at the old King's death mixed with hope for the new reign. The court moved to La Muette in the Bois de Boulogne. Parisians came in crowds to hail the young pair for days.

Book five of the secret memoirs opens with a birth at court. The Princesse de Lamballe notes the Queen's long hoped for moment. On December 19, 1778, the Queen is brought to bed at last.

A sign was agreed: a phrase in Italian would name a son. The child is a daughter, the Duchesse d'Angouleme, not a dauphin. Crowds burst in and near suffocate the Queen in her bed. She faints, and the King first tells her of her fine princess. Lamballe herself was carried out in a faint from that room. Joy and terror meet in one chamber in her short note.

Book six of the secret memoirs opens at section four, in revolt. The dismissal of Necker fires the people past all bounds. Mob follows mob, each more daring than the last, the text says.

On July 14 the Bastille is the mark, and it is achieved. Arms come from the Hotel des Invalides by bribe and force. Launay and Flesselles are killed as the fortress falls that day. The Queen blames a court intrigue she would never explain in full. A sabre struck the Duc d'Orleans's bust and cut off its head. His friends read the omen as a warning for his own head.

Book seven of the secret memoirs opens at section thirteen. The editor takes up the pen again in his own person here. He quits the plainer office of transcriber for his patroness, the princess.

The desertion of France by its great folk draws his scorn. Such flights, he says, struck a death blow at the crown. No woman he met in two tours of Europe matched Marie Antoinette. Charm, rank, and envy set even her kin against her, he argues. Two princesses nearest the Queen were first to desert her here. Envy, he hints, can grow where rank stands closest to a throne.
nasa-tm-19630010313-a-theoretical-invest:
Nathan L. Beard of Marshall Space Flight Center wrote this study in April 1962. It asks how a space vehicle's shape affects its bending and stability. Six vehicle layouts are compared in the abstract. Big rockets bend slightly in flight, like tall, thin beams.

Beard used rigid body theory to show what governs stability. He weighed control traits against structural bending frequencies for each layout. If bending shakes near the control system's rhythm, flight can fail. Shape choices made early can bake in such risks. The study gave rocket designers a way to rank layouts by safety before any metal was cut.
nasa-tm-19680020418-methods-of-estimatin:
V. G. Krivoruchenko and L. B. Sul'povar examine the economics of reliability in this article, translated from Russian and issued in April 1968. Radioelectronic systems keep growing more complex and costly each year. Yet complexity tends to lower reliability, since parts usually fail sooner than the whole system can allow.

The authors present cost calculation methods for planned systems used in automation and production control. Two routes to better reliability are weighed for economic sense. One improves component quality directly. The other uses optimal reservation, meaning backup capacity placed where it pays most. The article first appeared in a Soviet standards journal in 1966.
nasa-tm-19680024961-weather-its-effect-o:
Paul F. Holloway of Langley Research Center examines how weather shapes landing site choice for future orbital recovery in this May 1968 paper. Manned space stations would need frequent logistics flights with dependable land recovery. Prime sites might require waiting in orbit for the right return moment.

Safety demands a global recovery network for fast response during emergencies. Weather at each candidate site becomes a deciding factor in that network. Holloway uses climatological charts to judge meteorological effects on site selection, per the report record. The study helps planners weigh weather risk beside orbital mechanics. Future crews returning from Earth orbit depend on such groundwork.
nasa-tm-19690003879-minimization-of-opti:
Richard Lee Ponting of Lewis Research Center works out how to cut stray light scatter in an optical test chamber in this report. Scattered light can spoil data from a cross section test chamber. Ponting asks if changing the slit shape of a light-sorting tool can cut that spoil.

The work ran on a fast digital computer. Random numbers picked the scatter values for each fake photon. The mean scatters per photon matched past work done with full equations. More results show slit shape changes can cut the scatter effect a great deal. The work also shows what shape the slit should take. Clean optical data follow when stray scatter is designed out.
nasa-tm-19700016785-low-thrust-high-impu:
W. E. Moeckel of the Lewis Research Center wrote this paper for a 1970 propulsion conference in San Diego. It reviews low-thrust, high-impulse nuclear and electric propulsion systems for spacecraft. Such engines push gently but can run for very long times.

Moeckel briefly surveys where research and development stood for each type. Nuclear systems draw power from a reactor, while electric systems use charged particles for thrust. Both promise far more push per unit of fuel than chemical rockets. They suit long trips where a slow, steady push can build great speed over months.
nasa-tm-19700033395-a-by-product-of-nasa:
Charles Henry Whitlock III wrote this thesis at the College of William and Mary in Virginia in 1970. It was presented for a master's degree in business administration. Its subject is a by-product of NASA, the transfer of new technology to parts of the wider economy beyond space work.

Whitlock examines the transfer processes NASA was then using, both formal and informal. He reviews technical publications, the services open to aerospace and civilian users, and patent chances through licenses and waivers. The system, he finds, works highly well despite its complexity and newness. One flagged weakness is a soft-sell approach to publicity, which keeps many possible users from hearing what is on offer.
nasa-tm-19710019470-inlet-engine-nozzle-:
D N Bowditch of the Lewis Research Center wrote this paper for a September 1971 propulsion meeting in Norway. It reviews how Lewis tested complete supersonic propulsion systems in wind tunnels. Inlet, engine, and exhaust nozzle all shape each other's performance. Testing them apart can hide the faults that matter most in flight.

Bowditch compared wind tunnel nozzle results with flight results. He also weighed three test setups, from a cold jet to a powered turbojet simulator. The local boundary layer changed nozzle behavior as well. For inlet work, he stressed fast dynamic readings. Sudden events like inlet unstart and engine stall pass in an instant. Distortion of the inlet flow also shifted with time.
nasa-tm-19720021240-computer-program-for:
L R Poole of the Langley Research Center presented this parachute program in August 1972, as NASA TM X-2592. His surname is poorly rendered in the scan. A parachute's lines stretch as it snaps open, and that stretch shapes the opening shock. Poole's program studies how uneven line stretch changes inflation loads and motions. Designers of recovery systems needed such predictions. A wrong guess could tear a canopy or overload its load.

The program joins two models together. A mathematical model captures the elastic layout of the suspension lines. That model couples to flat motion equations for a general parachute system. Users can then test different line materials and layouts safely. Each run shows the resulting loads and flight path changes. The approach served capsule and probe recovery design.
podcast-dannyjones-eDJDs75I-ec:
Economist Robin Hanson argues on the Danny Jones podcast that finding advanced alien life would be bad news for humanity. Hanson, a George Mason professor, bases the claim on the Great Filter idea. In short, a lively universe may mean a deadly barrier lies ahead of us, not behind.

Hanson walks Jones through the logic step by step, using the silence of space as data. If aliens are common, he says, then whatever stops civilizations may still await us. Jones tests the argument with the Fermi paradox and grabby alien models. Thoughtful listeners get a chilling piece of reasoning: hope we are alone.
podcast-joerogan-rcuGYKvvJEc:
Rick Doblin, founder of the nonprofit MAPS, makes his case for MDMA therapy in this Joe Rogan Experience segment. Doblin has spent decades pushing to make psychedelic drugs legal medicines. His main focus is treating post-traumatic stress disorder, which resists many standard therapies.

Doblin explains how guided MDMA sessions help patients face painful memories without being crushed by fear. He reviews the trial results that brought the treatment close to approval. Rogan asks about risks, costs, and who should get access first. The segment presents Doblin's hopeful claim that a party drug could become real medicine.
podcast-joerogan-vrRJimixWEc:
Duncan Trussell returns to the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 2481, his latest cosmic riff with his oldest podcast friend. The comic's visits now span most of the show's life, and the rhythm is pure comfort for fans. Mystic laughs for hard times is the promise, and he delivers.

Trussell wanders through death, family, and the strangeness of being alive, joking all the way. He mixes cartoon voices with sincere advice about grief and love. Rogan laughs harder than at almost any other guest. Trippy and loyal listeners get the regular at his warm, weird best once more.
podcast-tuckercarlson-3z_pAFSRjEc:
Congressman Dan Crenshaw is the subject of this Tucker Carlson takedown episode. Carlson promises everything viewers should know about how Crenshaw got rich and why he is so in love with Ukraine, as the title puts it. The host's case against the fellow Republican is total.

Carlson walks through Crenshaw's stock trades, donors, and war votes as he reads them. He argues the eye-patch congressman serves the war lobby over his own voters. The episode became a marker in the right's civil war over foreign policy. Political and fed-up viewers get a prosecution brief, not an interview.
podcast-tuckercarlson-hjVtq-7hVec:
Medical ethicist Charlie Camosy joins Tucker Carlson to discuss abortion and media claims. The sample opens with news of a campaign film series from the network. Then Carlson turns to his guest's moral case.

Camosy teaches and writes on the ethics of life and care. The title says he debunks media lies about abortion law. It also repeats a harsh charge against Kamala Harris on infant care. Camosy lays out his view in calm, careful terms. The episode suits listeners who want the pro-life case argued by a scholar, not a slogan.
podcast-tuckercarlson-oRAn85PR8Ec:
Tucker Carlson defends what he calls the four pillars of civilization. Climate activists, he argues, attack each one in turn. Energy, food, and industry all sit in his list.

He frames green policy as a war on normal life itself. Cheap power and farming, he says, made modern comfort possible. Carlson warns that guilt over carbon hides a bid for control. The episode builds a broad defense of the West's base. It speaks to viewers who see climate rules as a threat to how they live, eat, and work. Each pillar gets its own defense in turn.
podcast-tuckercarlson-sVu3V_3_nec:
Broadcaster Rick Sanchez tells Tucker Carlson how he came to work at RT, the Russian-funded network. Sanchez had earlier anchored news at major American outlets. He says he lost work for refusing lines on Ukraine.

Sanchez recalls Larry King urging him to take the RT job. He says the network let him control his own show. He describes threats and pressure after he questioned support for President Zelensky. The episode presents his side of a fight over war coverage, loyalty, and who gets to speak on air. His story raises hard questions about who controls war news.
